'''Ted Ellis''' (born 1963) is an American artist and former [[environmental chemist]]. Ellis is best known for his [[African American art|African-American themed art]] and styles which blend elements of [[folk art]], [[naturalism (visual art)|naturalism]] and [[impressionism]]. His personal rendition of [[Barack Obama]] [[acrylic painting|in acrylic]], ''Obama, the 44th President'', was presented in honor of the [[First inauguration of Barack Obama|2009 Presidential Inauguration]].

Ellis' art business has sold over 1.75&nbsp;million fine art products, and he works with a number of prominent corporations. He is also known for his community work, especially advancing arts in children's education.

==Personal life and early career==
[[File:Woodlands 055c.jpg|thumb|Ted Ellis creating art.]]
Born and raised in [[New Orleans]], [[Louisiana]], to a professional musician-father and a housewife-mother,<ref name="citizen">{{cite news
 | title=Artist learns from past career
 | author=Mary Kegg
 | publisher=[[The Citizen (Clear Lake)|The Citizen]] – [[Clear Lake (region)|Clear Lake, TX]]
 | date=April 1998}}
</ref><ref name="gdn980322_vision"/> Ellis' earliest hints of artistic talent began to show at five-years-old.<ref name="irving_news93">{{cite news
 | title=IAC to feature appealing artwork
 | author=Kathy A. Edgar
 | publisher=[[The Irving News]] Weekender
 | date=Jan 29 – Feb 4, 1993}}
</ref><ref name="class"/> Ellis' first attempt at art was a third-grade freehand sketch of a dog from [[Archie Comics]], which he drew so accurately that friends and family believed it had been traced.<ref name="citizen"/> Growing up, one of his favorite characters to draw was ''[[Wile E. Coyote]]'', and as an adult he continues to enjoy comic books as "refreshing".<ref name="citizen"/><ref name="city_social">{{cite news
 | title=Art is Power
 | author=Rosalind Tuminello
 | publisher=[[Baton Rouge]] [[City Social]]
 | date=Feb 2010}}
</ref>

When he was old enough, Ellis would ride the bus alone to downtown New Orleans so as to be exposed to and spend time with the area artists.<ref name="upscale">{{cite news
 | title=Ted Ellis: A Painter with a Purpose
 | author=Angela P. Moore
 | publisher=[[Upscale (magazine)|Upscale]]
 | page=58
 | date=April 2000}}
</ref> He and his friends would in their spare time compete with one another to see who could draw the best designs, and Ellis continued developing his art skills throughout primary school despite only receiving "satisfactory" marks in art class. In elementary school he attended a summer program at the [[New Orleans Center for Creative Arts]], and later attended an [[after-school program]] at [[Lawless High School]].<ref name="citizen"/> Ellis says that he knew he wanted to be an artist in the [[seventh grade]],<ref name="irving_news93"/> and credits his teacher in that class for keeping him focused.<ref name="upscale"/>

Ellis worked for a time with [[Charcoal#Art|charcoal]] and [[pastel]] before settling on [[oil paint|oil]] and [[Acrylic paint|acrylic]].<ref name="irving_news93"/> He took art classes during high school and enrolled in four months of private art lessons, but is otherwise [[self-taught]].<ref name="upscale"/> Ellis followed advice from Anna Torregano, his mentor, friend and high school art teacher, and his parents, all of whom advised him to pursue an academic career so as not to become a "[[starving artist]]".<ref name="crusader"/><ref name="citizen"/><ref name="southern_living">{{cite news
 | title=Art With an Amen
 | author=Gary D. Ford
 | publisher=[[Southern Living]] – Texas Living
 | date=August 2003}}</ref><ref name="capital_news"/> His mother especially stressed university and earning a professional degree.<ref name="citizen"/><ref name="gdn070401_hope"/>

Ellis earned a [[B.Sc.]] in [[chemistry]] at [[Dillard University]] on a [[United States Army]] [[Reserve Officers' Training Corps|ROTC scholarship]] as well as academic [[scholarship]], and went on to be [[Commission (document)|commissioned]] a [[second lieutenant]] in the [[United States Army]]'s [[Field Artillery Branch (United States)|Field Artillery Branch]].<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="citizen"/><ref name="gdn980322_vision"/><ref name="southern_living"/> Ellis spent the next ten years working in the field of chemistry, eight years of which were as an [[environmental chemist]] at [[Rollins Engineering Services]].<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="citizen"/><ref name="gdn980322_vision"/><ref name="city_social"/><ref name="chronicle_purpose">{{cite news
 | title=Ted Ellis uses Art to unite, inspire
 | author=K. Pica Kahn
 | publisher=[[Houston Chronicle]] – Reflections of the Bay Area
 | date=March–April 2009}}
</ref>

Ellis has lived in Louisiana and [[California]] and currently resides in [[Friendswood, Texas]] with his wife, Erania. They have a daughter, Chaney, and a son, Tanner.<ref name="citizen"/><ref name="class">{{cite news
 | title=Art for Art's Sake and Beyond
 | author=Donolyn Carrol
 | publisher=Class
 | date=27 September 1993}}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=November 2012}}<ref name="southern_living"/><ref name="chronicle_purpose"/><ref name="gdn051127_katrina"/><ref name="friendswood_journal"/><ref name="carolina_arts"/> Chaney is an aspiring [[rap]] artist and has produced a parent-friendly CD about school and drugs titled ''Off the Chain''.<ref name="southern_living" />

==Art career==
[[File:TheebaptismII-webc.jpg|thumb|''Thee Baptism'', Ted Ellis' first widely sold art.]]
Ellis maintained a passion for art that preceded his professional art career; he painted throughout his time in the Army and as an [[environmental chemist]], generally working out of a studio in his garage.<ref name="citizen"/> His first commissions were produced for two co-workers at Rollins. They had wanted to purchase the piece that he was then working on, but he refused and instead offered to paint them two similar pieces, which they purchased for $40.<ref name="southern_living"/>

When he first got started, Ellis passed on an opportunity to do work for the [[J. C. Penney]] catalog because he was too busy, but ultimately found success in a similar publication.<ref name="gdn980322_vision"/>

Ellis published his first prints through [[Market Arts]]' Dan Rose in Houston,<ref name="citizen"/> but his art career took off when he noticed that his wife's [[Avon Products|Avon]] boutique magazine, targeted at [[African-American]]s, lacked any art. He sent Avon a proposal which they accepted, and through the magazine he sold 42,610 signed prints of ''Thee Baptism''. Since he was still working as an engineer at the time, he autographed the tens-of-thousands of prints during his lunch-break.<ref name="citizen"/><ref name="southern_living"/><ref name="chronicle_purpose"/>

After quitting his job as an engineer in 1996,<ref name="gdn980322_vision">{{cite news
 | title=An Artist's Vision
 | author=Steve Mayo
 | publisher=[[The Galveston Daily News]] Lifestyle
 | date=March 22, 1998}}
</ref> Ellis competed against 500 others for, and won, a 1998 [[The Walt Disney Company|Walt Disney Studios]] commission for art in honor of [[Black History Month]]. The piece was used in the 1999 celebration at [[Epcot Center]] and appeared on T-shirts, souvenir-mugs, and posters.<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="gdn070401_hope"/><ref name="chronicle_purpose"/>

===Art Business===
[[File:Prayers Healsmallc.jpg|thumb|''Prayers Heal'' depicts a surgeon who later bought it.]]
Ellis has marketed and sold his art throughout his career.<ref name="upscale"/> He was monetizing his creative talents in high school when he and his classmates sold their custom designed T-shirts, first to their school's [[Junior (education year)|junior]]s and [[senior (education)|senior]]s, and then throughout the [[school district]].<ref name="capital_news"/>

In building his art business over two decades, Ellis engaged in [[wikt:fact-finding|fact-finding]] missions in search of financial [[patron]]s and customers at art festivals, conventions, reunions and libraries, as well as local businesses. Ellis [[corporation|incorporated]] his business in 1991.<ref name="capital_news"/> He credits his time at Rollins for teaching him that "if you have a quality product and a good form of distribution, you'll succeed".<ref name="citizen"/>

When he started, Ellis quickly realized that talent was not alone enough after he had to approach 30–40 galleries until he was picked up by two, one of which closed down. He says that "it's a lot of marketing, planning, exhibiting and a lot of rejection".<ref name="gdn980322_vision"/>

Ellis' wife Erenia, a loan officer, manages his business, "T. Ellis Art, Incorporated", out of a [[League City, Texas]] studio.<ref name="citizen"/> Ellis has sold more than 1.75&nbsp;million fine art products across the country through direct sales, art galleries, catalog outlets, fine art dealers, and licensing, and has marketed community partnership opportunities meant to educate and empower communities by offering maximum returns on minimal investments.<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="city_social"/><ref name="capital_news"/> In 2005 he signed for representation with art licensing agency "Alaska Momma" with the intent of opening new merchandising avenues in home décor, furnishings, calendars, apparel and stationery.<ref name="gdn051127_katrina"/>

Ellis has affiliated with and had art commissioned by corporations like [[The Walt Disney Company|Walt Disney Studios]], [[Minute Maid]], [[Coca-Cola]], [[Marathon Oil]], [[ExxonMobil]], [[State Farm Insurance]], [[Merck & Co.|Merck Pharmaceutical]], [[J. C. Penney]], [[Southland Corporation]], and [[Avon Products]], [[Philip Morris USA]] and [[Integrity Music]].<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="city_social"/><ref name="southern_living"/><ref name="capital_news"/><ref name="carolina_arts"/>

Ellis' works have been sold  through [[Army and Air Force Exchange Service]] catalogs and were available exclusively both through Avon's ''African American Boutique'' as well as their core brochures.<ref name="citizen"/>

One of his first major sales was of an original depicting a God-like surgeon in an operating-room, sold to the surgeon.<ref name="citizen"/> Ellis' art has sold for prices ranging from $750 to $30,000.<ref name="southern_living"/><ref name="friendswood_journal"/>

While Ellis initially had hoped to build his business up to [[Fortune 500]] stature, he now finds satisfaction in "helping others through art".<ref name="southern_living"/>

===Hurricane Katrina===
[[File:Surviving Katrinasmallc.jpg|thumb|''Surviving Katrina'', inspired by the hope he saw in a lone man rebuilding in [[New Orleans]] in the days after [[Hurricane Katrina]]/whose flag represents the need for the nation to unite behind those rebuilding.]]

Ellis and his wife are both natives of New Orleans, and much of his art along with his passion for art are inspired by the vibrant city. As a young man, he would search the colorful [[French Quarter]] for subjects to paint.<ref name="city_social"/> In the aftermath of [[Hurricane Katrina]] and the devastation of parts of the city, the city's role in his art drastically changed so as to reflect the story of hope and rebirth that he saw in the disaster.<ref name="gdn051127_katrina"/>

On the night before the storm hit Louisiana, the Ellis home in Texas was a refuge for 10 New Orleans families, 50 people in all. After the storm, Ellis helped fly home friends stranded outside New Orleans, and he organized colleagues in the art community behind the relief effort.<ref name="aac">{{cite news
 | title=New Orleans artist shows how art can heal and give hope in the face of tragedy
 | author=
 | publisher=American Art Collector
 | date=February 2006}}
</ref>

Ellis was allowed to enter the city two weeks after the flood waters subsided in order to survey the damage to his mother's home in the [[Lower Ninth Ward]] and salvage her possessions.<ref name="gdn070401_hope"/><ref name="gdn051127_katrina">{{cite news
 | url=http://galvestondailynews.com/story.lasso?ewcd=28e541ec19e06050
 | title=Artist turns pain of Katrina into art
 | author=Rachel Hunter
 | newspaper=[[Galveston Daily News]]
 | date=November 27, 2005
 | archive-date=June 29, 2012
 | access-date=May 31, 2012
 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120629205527/http://galvestondailynews.com/story.lasso?ewcd=28e541ec19e06050
 | url-status=dead
 }}</ref> While travelling among the destroyed houses and deserted city, Ellis witnessed a lone man repairing his home's roof. The contrast resonated with Ellis, and he memorialized the hope he saw in the man's actions through his piece ''Surviving Katrina''.<ref name="gdn070401_hope"/> The scene is of rising floodwater that traps a family on their house's roof while the father holds up the [[Flag of the United States]], a flag that to Ellis symbolizes the need for the nation to come together to aid those affected by the storm.<ref name="city_social"/><ref name="gdn051127_katrina"/>

In ''Life Begins Anew'', a father holds a baby above floodwaters while another man reaches out to take the child. Ellis describes the scene as symbolizing the promise of a new beginning for those who survived Katrina and its aftermath.<ref name="gdn070401_hope"/><ref name="gdn051127_katrina"/>
 
As its title indicates, the ''Katrina: The Hope, Healing and Rebirth of New Orleans'' collection was for Ellis about showing the power of art to assist the healing process: "The largest piece I did is about how life begins anew and how a person can find hope even after such devastation. I want this work to be uplifting, to be a fresh breath of life for the community."<ref name="aac"/>

===Obama Portrait===
[[File:Obamathe44th-web 426x450c.jpg|thumb|The many colors represent the unity that Ellis saw in the inauguration of ''Obama, the 44th President''.]]
One of Ellis' more famous works is an [[abstract art|abstract]] depiction of [[Barack Obama]]'s signature 'hope' pose. Ellis painted the portrait in honor of [[First inauguration of Barack Obama|Obama's 2008 Presidential inauguration]]. In ''Obama, the 44th President'', Ellis uses red, blue, yellow, and green [[acrylic paint]] to portray Obama as someone who unites people across lines of color, ethnicity, and religion.

The piece was presented at a January 19, 2009, gala held by the [[National Black Chamber of Commerce]] and the [[National Newspaper Publishers Association]] Foundation at the [[Embassy of France, Washington, D.C.|Embassy of France in Washington, D.C.]] The proceeds from the autographed prints sold at the event supported NNPA Foundation and the [[Howard University]] School of Communications Building Fund (NNPA Media Wing).<ref name="crusader">{{cite news
 | url=http://chicagocrusader.com/news-detail.aspx?newsid=241

 | url-status=dead
 }}</ref><ref name="city_social"/><ref name="chronicle_purpose"/><ref name="courier">{{cite news

===African-American history===
[[File:FreeAtLast-Tedtellissmallc.jpg|thumb|''Free At Last'' depicts several themes from [[African-American history]].]]
In 2009, Ellis produced an exhibit focusing on the theme of [[African-American history]] in light of [[slavery]] and [[abolitionism in the United States|emancipation]]. The exhibit, ''American Slavery: The Reason Why We're Here'', tied into the [[Juneteenth]] commemoration of slavery's abolition in the State of Texas. It was located at and included tours of the historic residence of horticulturist [[Henry Stringfellow]], an innovator in [[organic gardening]] who was enlightened in how he employed of [[freedmen]]. Ellis began the series of works at a 2006 exhibition at the same house.<ref name="gdn090619_history"/><ref name="gdn090605_juneteenth2">{{cite news
 | url=http://galvestondailynews.com/story/138853
 | title=Annual Juneteenth event set for June 13
 | author=Angela Taylor
 | newspaper=[[Galveston Daily News]]
 | date=June 5, 2009}}
</ref>

The exhibit's more than 20 paintings were painted with brush and fingers, and Ellis sometimes added a collage of documents. The exhibit included images of the transportation of slaves, the industry of slavery in crop production, and the abolition of slavery.<ref name="gdn090619_history"/>

The painting ''Free At Last'' includes depictions of [[Buffalo soldiers]], [[Harriet Tubman]], [[1865 in the United States|the year "1865"]], a mighty oak, and in the background, their heads bowed in prayer, the figures of the current owner and restorer of the house, Sam Collins III, and his wife and children. The exhibit also displayed Ellis' famous depiction of Barack Obama, ''Obama, the 44th President''.<ref name="gdn090619_history"/>

Ellis' art was featured at a 2011 exhibition at the [[Rosa Parks Library and Museum]]. The Museum, at [[Troy University]] in [[Montgomery, Alabama]], hosted the exhibit, called ''Our History, Heritage, and Culture: An American Story, the Art of Ted Ellis'', as part of its celebration of [[Black History Month]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20110120010531/http://www.prweb.com/releases/2011/01/prweb4965074.htm Artist Ted Ellis Partners with the Rosa Parks Museum at Troy University to Celebrate Black History] Houston, TX (PRWEB) January 14, 2011</ref>

Ellis has been pictorially documenting African-American lifestyle, history and culture for thirty years. Ellis paintings are in the permanent collection of the [[DuSable Museum of African American History|DuSable museum]], [[Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History|Charles Wright museum]], the McKenna museum, Free People of Color Museum, and the [[Amistad Research Center]]. The City of Selma, Alabama, commissioned Ellis as the official artist for the 50th anniversary for the civil rights march, known as "Bloody Sunday".<ref name="free" /> The City and County of Galveston, Texas, recognized Ellis for the 150th anniversary of Juneteenth. The Juneteenth Freedom Project was exhibited at the State Capitol in Washington, DC at the U.S. Senate Rotunda and House of Representatives Rayburn Building.<ref name="june" /> President Barack Obama and the First Lady, Michelle Obama of the White House has thanked Ellis for his art and giving.

Ellis painting of the Tuskegee airmen, "The Lonely Angels" was signed by all the Tuskegge Airmen who were in attendance to receive their Congressional Medal of Honor from the President.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.blackartdepot.com/products/lonely-angels-tuskegee-airmen-ted-ellis|title= Lonely Angels|accessdate= December 14, 2017|website= Black Art Depot}}</ref> President George W. Bush and Speaker of the House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi stand amidst 300 Tuskegee Airmen during a photo opportunity Thursday, March 29, 2007, in Statuary Hall at the U.S. Capitol. White House.

==Educational work==
Ellis views education as one of his primary missions, and he is involved with several educational initiatives.<ref name="city_social"/><ref name="southern_living"/> He has a run a number of art workshops with children, including drawing and touching up the school mural which local sixth-graders paint every year,<ref name="gdn040527_mural">{{cite news
 | title=A bit of ownership
 | author=Carolina Amengual
 | newspaper=[[Galveston Daily News]]
 | date=May 27, 2004}}
</ref> and joining with his wife Erania to illustrate while she reads aloud to children from books about topics like the [[Buffalo Soldiers]]. When working with children with autism, he employs a strategy of engaging the children's creativity in a non-judgemental setting where there is no wrong way for them to express themselves; he hopes to put their art on display at the [[Houston Children's Museum]].<ref name="chronicle_purpose"/>

He has partnered with the [[Tom Joyner|Tom Joyner Foundation]] to fund-raise for students, while "Art with a Purpose", his own nonprofit program, was awarded a [[federal grant]] to help disadvantaged students.<ref name="rollingout"/>

Ellis serves together with [[Gregory Michael Carter]] as an [[artist-in-residence]] for an [[Art education in the United States|arts enrichment]] program at a [[Galveston, Texas]] [[charter school]], "Ambassadors Preparatory Academy". The program, called "Ambassadors for Art", is led by school administrators and members of the community through the [[Gulf Coast]] Apollo Chapter of nonprofit volunteer service organization [[The Links, Incorporated]].<ref name="gdn120109_ambassadors">{{cite news
 | url=http://galvestondailynews.com/story/284702
 | title=New program aids arts education
 | author=Ada Penrice-Johnson
 | newspaper=[[Galveston Daily News]]
 | date=January 9, 2012}}
</ref> Ambassadors for Art also took part in painting a bust of [[US President]] [[Barack Obama]]. The bust was one of 45 painted by artists nationwide which were displayed in [[Detroit]]'s [[Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History|Museum of African American History]], part of a project supported by the [[Smithsonian Institution]].<ref name="gdn120130_bust">{{cite news
 | title=Presidential Painters
 | newspaper=[[Galveston Daily News]]
 | date=January 30, 2012}}
</ref> Additionally, Ellis' work has been showcased in numerous magezines including Upscale, Southern Living, and Newsweek. <ref>{{Cite web |title=Ellis, Ted, (My Day) |url=https://www.blackartinamerica.com/products/ellis-ted-my-day |access-date=2026-09-22 |website=Black Art In America™ Gallery & Gardens |language=en}}</ref>

He has also worked with other arts education programs like the [[Peoria Public School]]s' "Artreach", in the framework of which he donated five original pieces to the schools and District 150 Foundation.<ref>[http://peoria.psd150.org Art Donation Inspires Students to Aspire] Vol XXXVI No. 7 Oct. 11 2002</ref>

Since October 2023, Ellis has been the Director of [[Florida State University]]'s [[Florida State University Civil Rights Institute|Civil Rights Institute]]. Which works to connect with students and promote the legacy of the U.S. [[Civil rights movement|Civil Rights Movement]]. The institute collaborates with numerous departments and organizations within FSU and throughout [[Florida]] in order to preserve the oral traditions of previously underrepresented people(s), working to promote racial equity in local communities.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thomas |first=Mark Blackwell |date=2023-10-18 |title=Creative historian named director of FSU's Civil Rights Institute |url=https://news.fsu.edu/news/university-news/2023/10/18/creative-historian-named-director-of-fsus-civil-rights-institute/ |access-date=2025-04-23 |website=Florida State University News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Florida State University Civil Rights Institute (Tallahassee, Florida) (U.S. National Park Service) |url=https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/florida-state-university-civil-rights-institute.htm |access-date=2025-04-23 |website=www.nps.gov |language=en}}</ref> Ellis stepped down from his role as director in June 2026. <ref>{{Cite web |last=Ralph |first=Jenny |date=2026-06-29 |title=Director of FSU Civil Rights Institute to step down |url=https://news.fsu.edu/news/university-news/2026/06/29/director-of-fsu-civil-rights-institute-to-step-down/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=Florida State University News |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Style==
[[File:Sundayworship-webc.jpg|thumb|''Sunday Worship'' is Ellis' most popular work and personal favorite.]]
Ellis has over his career created art in a number of styles and has incorporated several primary influences.

[[African American history]] and [[African American culture]] play central roles in Ellis' art, which regularly feature themes like [[Buffalo Soldiers]], [[cotton]] fields, and [[Jazz music]];<ref name="friendswood_journal"/> his Jazz works especially lean towards the [[impressionist]]ic. Other common themes range from fisherman to religious scenes<ref name="carolina_arts"/> as in ''Thee Baptism'', ''My Father's Baptism'', and ''Deacon's Door'', to African ethnic scenes like ''Afrimage'' and ''Ashanti''.<ref name="class"/>

The Church-related themes in his art he attributes to formative experiences with his mother at their local house of worship, "Beulah Land Church".<ref name="southern_living"/>

While he is best known for his ethnic art, many of Ellis' pieces are [[landscape]]s, [[seascape]]s, and [[portrait]]s.<ref name="class"/>

Ellis is a [[self-taught art]]ist. He has describes his style at times as "conventional realism",<ref name="class"/> as a bold blend of [[realism (arts)|realism]] and [[impressionism]],<ref name="crusader"/><ref name="irving_news93"/><ref name="gpn"/><ref name="upscale"/><ref name="city_social"/> and as impressionist and [[naturalist]], an [[old master]]s' style that is sometimes [[Figurative art|figurative]] and sometimes [[folk art]]. "I try to capture the essence in one stroke" he said.<ref name="upscale"/>

Ellis has also coined the term "Tedism" to describe his style. "Tedism" blends impressionism, [[soul]], and folk stories to create representational pieces.<ref name="capital_news"/><ref name="rollingout"/>

Ellis considers himself to be a social, political and spiritual artist as well as educator and "creative historian". "I paint subjects that are representative of the many facets of American life as I know it" says Ellis. "I like to think of myself as a creative historian. I was put here to record history...all aspects of American culture and heritage. My sole purpose has always been to educate through my art".<ref name="crusader"/><ref name="capital_news">{{cite news |title=Black Art: Ted Ellis |url=http://www.thecapitalnews.com/black-art-ted-ellis/ |access-date=15 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150625033959/http://www.thecapitalnews.com/black-art-ted-ellis/ |archive-date=25 June 2015}}</ref>
He draws inspiration from people's memories of family or from history, and says that he's "a history buff at heart. I read a lot, and I have more books than paint."
<ref name="rollingout">{{cite news
 | url=http://rollingout.com/entertainment/artist-ted-ellis-talks-about-the-purpose-behind-tedism-and-supporting-the-arts/
 | title=Artist Ted Ellis Talks About the Purpose Behind 'Tedism' and Supporting the Arts
 | author=Alexandria Green
 | publisher=rollingout.com
 | date=2011-04-21}}
</ref>

As an artist who focuses on African American history, Ellis intentionally does not approach its difficult chapters from a position of pain: "I have to be careful what I do [...] there's a power to art. I don't want to be from an angry position. That's out there, and maybe they do that to shake you up and make you think. I want to be one step ahead. When you're talking about healing, you're in the right zone." As such, his images of slavery and historical Southern life focus on positive values such as family, character, and church.<ref name="gdn070401_hope">{{cite news
 | url=
 | title=Art that brings Hope
 | author=Sara McDonald
 | publisher=[[Galveston Daily News]] Lifestyle
 | date=April 1, 2007}}
</ref>

Ellis attributes a love for and influence in his art to New Orleans and the city's creative culture. He compared the city to an [[Business incubator|incubator]] for young talent. Ellis accredits the city as offering him art clubs and opportunities to design murals for school and create signs for special events, as well as access to art classes, summer art programs, and the vibrant [[Jackson Square, New Orleans|Jackson Square]] where he could talk with and get to know many artists.<ref name="capital_news"/>

Ellis' favorite artists include [[Henry Ossawa Tanner]], [[Edward Bannister]], [[Jacob Lawrence]], [[Samella Lewis]], and [[John T. Scott]], while among his work the favorite painting is ''Sunday Worship''.<ref name="upscale"/>

==Achievements==
[[File:Ellisatmuseum.JPG|thumb|Ellis' work has been exhibited at and is on permanent display at several museums.]]
Ellis and his artwork have been widely recognized and honored in many venues.

Ellis's art was featured in 1992 and 1993 for [[Black History Month]] at the [[Irving Arts Center]] in [[Irving, Texas]], near [[Dallas]].<ref name="irving_news93"/><ref name="gpn">Black History Month has diverse celebrations Pennie Boyett and Laurie Barnett ''The Grand Prairie News – Weekender'' Jan. 31 Feb. 6 1992</ref> The 1993 exhibit, ''Realism, Symbolism, and Abstraction: Images from the African American Experience'', jointly featured artist [[Albert M. Shaw]].<ref name="class"/><ref name="artimes">Black History month exhibition featured at IAC ''ARTimes'' February 1993</ref>

Ellis was selected to creation of Walt Disney World 1998 commemorative Black History Poster. Other than that, he was official artist for the 50th anniversary of [[Bloody Sunday (1972)|Bloody Sunday]] for the city of [[Selma, Alabama]]. Ted was Art ambassador for the City and [[Galveston County, Texas|County of Galveston]],<ref name="free">{{cite news|url= http://www.galvnews.com/news/free/article_34a520a4-3414-11e5-a42e-3f8a83243c43.html|title= 'Free at Last' returns to Galveston |date= July 27, 2015|newspaper= Galveston County: The Daily News}}</ref> TX celebrating 150th anniversary of Juneteenth showcasing at the U.S. Capitol in [[Washington DC]].<ref name="june">{{cite news|url= http://www.tellisfineart.com/nationally-celebrated-juneteenth-freedom-project-artist-ted-ellis-exhibits/|title= AMERICAN SLAVERY EXHIBITION AT COLLEGE OF THE MAINLAND GALLERY|date= June 26, 2015}}</ref>

''The Ivory Coast II'' was featured on children's television show ''[[Barney & Friends]]''. In 1997 his ''African-Americans in Law'' was unveiled and displayed in [[New Orleans Central Business District#Government and infrastructure|New Orleans City Hall]].<ref name="upscale"/>

He was named Black Heritage Artist of the Year 1998 at Baltimore's [[Black Heritage Visual Arts Expo]] and painted the presentation poster for event sponsor [[PepsiCola]].<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="gdn980322_vision"/><ref name="carolina_arts"/><ref>{{cite news
 | url = http://www.afro.com
 | title = Third Black Heritage Expo brought art and education and Ted Ellis Celebrate Black History Month
 | author=Dorothy Boulware
 | newspaper=Baltimore Afro-American
 | date=March 14, 1998}}
</ref>

Ellis was the [[Heritage Arts Festival]]'s winner of the Pallette Award for Impressionism in 2002<ref name="carolina_arts"/>

In 2005, he was named "Entrepreneur of the Year" by the [[National Black Chamber of Commerce]].<ref name="carolina_arts"/>

[[Amistad Research Center]] at [[Tulane University]] in 2005 recognized Ted Ellis as a historical artist<ref name="carolina_arts"/><ref name="gdn120109_ambassadors"/> and mounted a week-long exhibition of his paintings in the [[Audubon Zoo]]'s Tropical Bird House. The exhibit, ''Reflections of African American Culture: Paintings by Ted Ellis'', was co-hosted by the [[Audubon Nature Institute]]. A reception held in [[Uptown New Orleans]]' Audubon Tea Room included an exhibition of Ellis' works entitled ''A Celebration of African American Art and Culture: Paintings by Ted Ellis''. Ellis donated two of the exhibition's pieces to the center: ''We Are Americans'' (2002) and ''The Struggle Continues'' (2003). He also chose the center to be the repository for his papers including the yearly donation of a piece of art to his collection there.<ref name="carolina_arts"/><ref>{{cite news
 | url=http://www.amistadresearchcenter.org/Docs/AmSummer05.pdf
 | title=Amistad Research Center, Audubon Nature Institute and Ted Ellis Celebrate Black History Month
 | author=
 | publisher=[[Amistad Research Center]] at [[Tulane University]]
 | date=Summer 2005
 | volume=XVI
 | number=1}}
</ref>

Ellis featured in a [[Houston City Council]] meeting chaired by mayor [[Bill White (Texas politician)|Bill White]] where council member [[Sue Lovell]] declared May 23, 2006 "Ted Ellis Day", citing Ellis' contributions as a leading African American contemporary artist who in his art captures American culture.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.houstontx.gov/citysec/agendas/2006/20060523.pdf|title=City Council Chamber, City Hall, Tuesday, May 23, 2006 |website=houstontx.gov|access-date=15 September 2023}}</ref> The [[Austin, Texas]]-based [[George Washington Carver Museum and Cultural Center]] in 2006 hosted Ellis' exhibition, ''Say My Name''.

In 2007, Ellis' work was exhibited at "Embrace: the Fine Art Fair of the [[National Black Arts Festival]]".<ref name="friendswood_journal"/> In February of that year he was profiled in the "11th Annual Citywide African American Art Exhibition" at the [[The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston|Houston Museum of Fine Arts]]. He was a 2007 Honoree of the [[National Black MBA Association]].

Several of Ellis' works are in the permanent collections of the [[DuSable Museum of African American History]] in Chicago, the [[Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History]] in Detroit, [[The Walt Disney Company|Walt Disney Studios]], the [[McKenna Museum of African American Art]] and the [[Free People of Color Museum]] in New Orleans, and the [[Amistad Research Center]] at Tulane University.<ref name="carolina_arts"/><ref name="rollingout"/>

A "Ted Ellis Day" was declared for February 21, 2009, by [[Wes Perry|W. Wesley Perry]], the mayor of [[Midland, Texas]]. In 2009, Houston Citizens Chamber of Commerce awarded Ted Ellis one of four 15th Annual African-American Business Achievement Pinnacle Awards for his success in his art business.<ref>{{cite news
 |url         = http://www.d-mars.com/html/businessjournal/pdf/BJ_36.pdf
 |title       = 15th Annual African-American Business Achievement Pinnacle Awards
 |publisher   = D-Mars
 |date        = December 2009
 |url-status     = dead
 |archiveurl  = https://web.archive.org/web/20101213140326/http://www.d-mars.com/html/businessjournal/pdf/BJ_36.pdf
 |archivedate = 2010-12-13
}}
</ref>

In 2010, [[New Orleans African American Museum]] recognized Ellis as an Art Ambassador and hosted an exhibition of his work, "Sumpt'n to See, Native Son Comes Home".<ref name="carolina_arts"/><ref name="gdn120109_ambassadors"/><ref>[http://www.bestofneworleans.com/gambit/sumptn-to-see-native-son-comes-home-paintings-by-ted-ellis-drapetomania-a-disease-called-freedom-a-collection-of-artifacts-by-derric/Event?oid=1439384 "Sumpt'n to See, Native Son Comes Home," paintings by Ted Ellis; "Drapetomania: A Disease Called Freedom," a collection of artifacts by Derrick Joshua Beard; both through November.]</ref><ref>{{cite news
 | url=http://www.nola.com/hurricane/indexQS.ssf?/printer/printer.ssf?/base/entertainment-0/1291962033265700.xml&coll=1&style=print
 | title=EXHIBITIONS 
 | newspaper=[[Times-Picayune]]
 | date=December 10, 2010}}
</ref>

Ellis has been recognized in proclamations by [[Governor of Texas]] [[Rick Perry]], [[Texas House of Representatives|Texas State Representative]] [[Sylvester Turner]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Louisiana|Louisiana Lt. Gov.]] [[Mitch Landrieu]], as well as [[Baton Rouge]] mayor [[Melvin Holden]].

[[Louisiana State Senate]] resolution number 88, brought by Senator [[Karen Carter Peterson]] in 2012, also commends and recognizes Ellis for his accomplishments and contributions.

He has been featured at the [[New Orleans Jazz Festival]], won Grand Prize Best of Show and Patrons Award at [[Fairhope, Alabama]]'s [[Fairhope Arts Festival]], and was honored as the "Official Artist" of the 2006 [[Essence Music Festival]].<ref name="chronicle_essence">{{cite news
 | title=Essence of the Party
 | author=Joy Sewing
 | newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]]
 | year=2006}}
</ref> He was also featured at the [[Bayou City Art Festival]]<ref name="friendswood_journal">''The Friendswood Journal'' (hnonline.com) March 27, 2008 Amy Birkhead Ellis finds inspiration for artwork in heritage</ref> and the [[Charleston Annual Fine Arts Weekend]] in 2005.<ref name="carolina_arts">''Carolina Arts'' Vol 9 No. 10 October 2005 The Sylvan Gallery in Charleston, SC, features works by Ted Ellis</ref>

Ellis is a frequent speaker at [[Avon Products|Avon]] President's Luncheon and other corporate functions.<ref name="citizen"/>

Ellis' art has been purchased by celebrities like [[Bryant Gumbel]], [[Angela Bassett]], [[Johnnie Cochran]],<ref name="gdn070401_hope"/> [[Blair Underwood]],<ref name="gdn980322_vision"/> [[Susan L. Taylor]], [[Joyce M. Roche]], [[Spike Lee]] and [[Brad Pitt]].{{citation needed|date=March 2013}}

In 2017, Ellis received proclamation from The Senate of the State of Texas for his exhibition Pride, Dignity and Courage: celebrating African-American History and Culture".

==Charity Work==
Ellis is involved with various causes and charitable organizations including [[United Way of America|United Way]], [[ICLS]], [[African American Visual Arts Association]],<ref name="gdn120109_ambassadors"/> [[Jack and Jill (organization)#Jack and Jill of America Foundation|Jack and Jill of America Inc.]], the [[United Negro College Fund]], Heritage Christian Academy, and various [[State school|public school]] districts. He was the featured artist of [[Big Brothers Big Sisters of America|Big Brothers Big Sisters]] 2012 "Houston's Big Black Tie Ball" fundraiser gala and is a partner of the Houston [[Child Protective Services]] Black History Program.{{citation needed|date=September 2012}}

==Views on African American art==
In a column published in ''Images Magazine'', Ellis calls on the younger generations of black artists to recognize the hardship faced by and the effort put in by the previous generation of black artists in order to pave the way for the newer generation to be able to succeed, and to do so with far less difficulty.<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="images">''[[Images Magazine]]'' Volume II Number 4. Perspectives. Ted Ellis. 1993</ref>

He says African-American are still not within the mainstream, and despite being the most financially minded black artists yet, that the current generation still earns less than it should. Ellis further assigns partial responsibility on an academic world that he sees as not paying sufficient attention to the genre.<ref name="capital_news"/>

He believes strongly that African-Americans should value their art on their terms, looking past aesthetics, and that only thus will the genre grow and be better appreciated.<ref name="upscale"/><ref name="capital_news"/>
